syllabusOutcomes.6.1: Know and use properties and graphs of logarithmic and exponential functions, including ln x and e^x; asymptotes; graphs of y = ke^{nx} + a and y = k ln(ax+b)
syllabusOutcomes.6.2: Know and use the laws of logarithms, including change of base
syllabusOutcomes.6.3: Solve equations of the form a^x = b

groups.label: ln and e as inverse functions

questions.statement: Given that \(\;\log_3 r + 2\log_9 s = 8\), find the value of \(rs\). [3]
tips: Two different bases (3 and 9) — convert to ONE base first: \(\log_9 s = \dfrac{\log_3 s}{\log_3 9} = \dfrac{\log_3 s}{2}\).
So \(2\log_9 s = \log_3 s\): the equation collapses to \(\log_3 r + \log_3 s = 8\).
Adding logs multiplies the arguments: \(\log_3(rs) = 8 \Rightarrow rs = 3^8\).
solution: Change base 9 to base 3: \(\log_9 s = \dfrac{\log_3 s}{\log_3 9} = \dfrac{\log_3 s}{2}\), so \(2\log_9 s = \log_3 s\).
markScheme: B1 — \(2\log_9 s = \dfrac{2\log_3 s}{\log_3 9}\) soi (change of base, any consistent base)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write \(1 + \lg(x^2-1) - 2\lg(x-1)\), where \(x>1\), as a single logarithm to base 10. Give your answer in its simplest form.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Solve the equation \(4\log_5(x+1) = 9\log_{(x+1)}5\), giving your answers in the form \(a+b\sqrt{c}\), where \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are constants.

questions.statement:
(a) Write \(\;1 + \lg(x^2-1) - 2\lg(x-1)\), where \(x>1\), as a single logarithm to base 10. Give your answer in its simplest form. [4]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;4\log_5(x+1) = 9\log_{(x+1)}5\), giving your answers in the form \(a+b\sqrt{c}\). [5]
tips: (a) Convert the lone number first: \(1 = \lg 10\). Convert the coefficient: \(2\lg(x-1) = \lg(x-1)^2\).
(a) Factorise inside: \(x^2-1 = (x-1)(x+1)\) — that is what makes the final fraction "simplest": one \((x-1)\) cancels.
(b) \(\log_{(x+1)}5\) is the RECIPROCAL of \(\log_5(x+1)\) (change of base). Let \(u = \log_5(x+1)\): the equation becomes \(4u = \dfrac9u\).

(b) \(u^2 = \tfrac94 \Rightarrow u = \pm\tfrac32\) — do NOT forget the negative root: it gives the second answer. Undo with \(x+1 = 5^{u}\) and use \(5^{3/2} = 5\sqrt5\), \(5^{-3/2} = \tfrac{1}{5\sqrt5} = \tfrac{\sqrt5}{25}\).
solution: (b) Change of base: \(\log_{(x+1)}5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5(x+1)}\). With \(u = \log_5(x+1)\): \(4u = \dfrac9u \Rightarrow u^2 = \dfrac94 \Rightarrow u = \pm\dfrac32\).
(Both are valid: \(x+1>0\) and \(x+1\neq1\) in each case.)
markScheme: (a) B1 — \(1=\lg10\) soi; M1 — correct use of a log rule; DM1 — factorises \(x^2-1\) and simplifies; A1 — \(\lg\frac{10(x+1)}{x-1}\)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write \(3 + 4\log_2 a - \log_2 b\) as a single base 2 logarithm.

questions.statement:
(a) Write \(\;3 + 4\log_2 a - \log_2 b\;\) as a single base 2 logarithm. [3]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;\lg x = 4\log_x 10\). [4]
tips: (a) Convert the number to a log in the right base: \(3 = \log_2 8\). Power rule: \(4\log_2 a = \log_2 a^4\).
(b) \(\log_x 10 = \dfrac{1}{\lg x}\) (reciprocal — change of base with the roles swapped).
(b) So \((\lg x)^2 = 4 \Rightarrow \lg x = \pm2\). TWO answers: \(x = 10^2\) and \(x = 10^{-2}\).
Keep the ± — dropping the negative square root is the classic mark-loser in this question type.
solution: (b) \(\log_x 10 = \dfrac{1}{\lg x}\), so \(\lg x = \dfrac{4}{\lg x} \Rightarrow (\lg x)^2 = 4 \Rightarrow \lg x = \pm 2\).
\(\lg x = 2 \Rightarrow x = 100\); \(\lg x = -2 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{100}\). (Both valid: positive and \(\neq 1\).)
markScheme: (a) B1 — \(3=\log_2 8\); M1 — correct use of two log operations; A1 — \(\log_2\frac{8a^4}{b}\)
(b) B1 — change of base: \(\lg x = \frac{4}{\lg x}\) oe
(b) B1 — \((\lg x)^2 = 4\) (dep; must work with \((\lg x)^2\), not \(\lg x^2\))

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write \(5\lg a - 4\lg b - 3\) as a single base 10 logarithm.

questions.statement:
(a) Write \(\;5\lg a - 4\lg b - 3\;\) as a single base 10 logarithm. [3]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;\log_5(x+1) - \log_{(x+1)}5 = 0\). [4]
tips: (a) \(-3 = -\lg 1000\): subtracting a log divides — the 1000 goes to the denominator.
(b) Reciprocal trick again: \(\log_{(x+1)}5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5(x+1)}\), so \((\log_5(x+1))^2 = 1\).
(b) \(\log_5(x+1) = \pm1\): \(x+1 = 5\) or \(x+1 = \tfrac15\). The mark scheme explicitly penalises rejecting \(x = -\tfrac45\) — it IS valid because \(x+1 = \tfrac15 > 0\).
markScheme: (a) B2 — \(\lg(a^5 \div b^4 \div 1000)\) partial forms (B1 for \(3=\lg1000\) soi and B1 power rule); final \(\lg\frac{a^5}{1000b^4}\)
(b) A1 — \(x=4\);  A1 — \(x=-\frac45\) (A0 if rejected or crossed out)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write \(\dfrac{1}{\log_x e} - \ln(x-1)\) as a single logarithm to base e.

questions.statement:
(a) Write \(\;\dfrac{1}{\log_x \mathrm{e}} - \ln(x-1)\;\) as a single logarithm to base e. [2]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;2\log_5 2x = 1 + \log_5(9x-10)\). [5]
tips: (a) The reciprocal rule in reverse: \(\dfrac{1}{\log_x e} = \ln x\). Then subtract: \(\ln x - \ln(x-1) = \ln\dfrac{x}{x-1}\).
(b) Power rule first: \(2\log_5 2x = \log_5(2x)^2 = \log_5 4x^2\) — square the WHOLE \(2x\), not just \(x\)!
(b) Replace \(1 = \log_5 5\), combine the right side, then equate arguments: \(4x^2 = 5(9x-10)\).
(b) Solve the quadratic and CHECK both answers in the original logs (arguments must be positive).
solution: (a) \(\dfrac{1}{\log_x e} = \ln x\) (change of base), so the expression is \(\ln x - \ln(x-1) = \ln\dfrac{x}{x-1}\).

tips: Bases 2 and 16 — link them: \(16 = 2^4\), so \(\log_{16}x = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{4}\).
\(\log_2 x^2 = 2\log_2 x\). The equation becomes \(\left(2 + \tfrac14\right)\log_2 x = 18\), i.e. \(\tfrac94\log_2 x = 18\).
Finish with the definition: \(\log_2 x = 8 \Rightarrow x = 2^8\).
solution: Change base: \(\log_{16}x = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 16} = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{4}\), and \(\log_2 x^2 = 2\log_2 x\).
markScheme: M3 — correctly derives an equation free of logarithms, e.g. \(x^9 = 16^{18}\) or \(x^{9/4} = 2^{18}\) (M2 for consistent bases + one correct log law in a correct equation; M1 for one of these steps)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write down the set of values of \(x\) for which \(\log_5(12x-4)\) exists.

questions.statement:
(a) Write down the set of values of \(x\) for which \(\log_5(12x-4)\) exists. [1]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;\log_5(12x-4) = \dfrac{6}{\log_x 125} + 1\). [6]
tips: (a) A logarithm exists only for a POSITIVE argument: \(12x-4>0\).
(b) \(\log_x 125 = 3\log_x 5 = \dfrac{3}{\log_5 x}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{\log_x 125} = 2\log_5 x = \log_5 x^2\).
(b) Replace \(1 = \log_5 5\), combine: \(\log_5(12x-4) = \log_5 5x^2\) → drop the logs.
(b) The quadratic gives \(x = \tfrac25\) and \(x = 2\) — both survive the checks (both exceed \(\tfrac13\), both valid bases). Part (a) is your checking tool!
solution: (b) \(\log_x 125 = \dfrac{3}{\log_5 x}\), so \(\dfrac{6}{\log_x 125} = 2\log_5 x\). The equation becomes
Both are \(> \tfrac13\) (part (a)) and are valid bases (\(>0, \neq 1\)): both solutions stand.
markScheme: (b) B1 — change of base: \(\frac{6}{\log_x 125} = 2\log_5 x\) oe

questions.statement:
(a) Write down the value of \(\lg(10\,000)\). [1]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;\log_2(\log_3 x) = 2\). [3]

(c) Solve the equation \(\;\log_x 5 = \log_5 x^4\). [4]
tips: (b) Unwrap nested logs from the OUTSIDE in: \(\log_2(\square)=2 \Rightarrow \square = 2^2 = 4\), then \(\log_3 x = 4\).
(c) \(\log_x 5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x}\) and \(\log_5 x^4 = 4\log_5 x\): a quadratic in \(u=\log_5 x\): \(\dfrac1u = 4u\).
(c) \(u^2 = \tfrac14 \Rightarrow u = \pm\tfrac12\) — both roots give valid answers: \(x = 5^{1/2} = \sqrt5\) and \(x = 5^{-1/2} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\). Keep both!
solution: \(x = 5^{1/2} = \sqrt5\) or \(x = 5^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\). Both are positive and \(\neq 1\): both valid.
markScheme: (c) B1 — \(\log_x 5 = \frac{1}{\log_5 x}\) (or both sides to a common base) soi
(c) B1 — \((\log_5 x)^2 = \frac14\); B1 — \(x=\sqrt5\); B1 — \(x=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\) oe (do not reject either)

questions.statement:
(a) Solve the equation \(\;\log_5(5x-2) - \log_{25} x = \dfrac12\). [5]

(b) Solve the equation \(\;\mathrm{e}^{3y-7} + \dfrac{4}{\mathrm{e}^3} = \dfrac{5}{\mathrm{e}^{3y-1}}\). [6]
tips: (a) \(\log_{25}x = \dfrac{\log_5 x}{2}\). Double everything (or write \(\tfrac12 = \log_5\sqrt5\)) and combine into one log each side.
(a) The resulting quadratic \(25x^2-25x+4=0\) has roots \(\tfrac45\) AND \(\tfrac15\) — but \(x=\tfrac15\) makes \(5x-2 = -1 < 0\): reject it. Answer: \(x=\tfrac45\) only. Always test log arguments!
(b) Multiply through by \(e^{3y-1}\) (or spot the quadratic in \(e^{3y-4}\)): you get \(e^{6y-8} + 4e^{3y-4} - 5 = 0\).
(b) Factorise as \((e^{3y-4}-1)(e^{3y-4}+5) = 0\); the exponential can't equal \(-5\), so \(e^{3y-4}=1 \Rightarrow 3y-4=0\).
solution: Check: \(x=\tfrac15 \Rightarrow 5x-2 = -1 < 0\) — the original log does not exist. Reject. So \(x = \tfrac45\) only.
markScheme: (a) B1 — change of base \(\log_{25}x=\frac{\log_5 x}{2}\); B1 — \(2\log_5(5x-2)=\log_5(5x-2)^2\)
(a) M1 — \(\log_5\frac{(5x-2)^2}{x}=1\) (dep); M1 — \(25x^2-25x+4=0\) with attempt to solve (dep)
(a) A1 — \(x=\frac45\) ONLY (the root \(\frac15\) must be rejected)
(b) B1 — combined equation oe; B1 — 3-term quadratic \(e^{6y-8}+4e^{3y-4}-5[=0]\) (dep)

questions.statement:
On the axes, sketch the graph of \(\;y = 5\ln(4x+3)\).
State the intercepts with the axes.
State the equation of any asymptote. [4]
tips: Three things earn the marks: shape, intercepts, asymptote — compute all three BEFORE drawing.
Vertical asymptote where the inside hits zero: \(4x+3=0 \Rightarrow x=-\tfrac34\). The curve dives to \(-\infty\) there.
\(x\)-intercept where the inside equals 1 (since \(\ln 1 = 0\)): \(4x+3=1 \Rightarrow x=-\tfrac12\).
\(y\)-intercept at \(x=0\): \(y = 5\ln 3\) — leave it exact.
Shape: an increasing ln curve, steep near the asymptote, flattening as \(x\) grows — no maximum, no second branch.
solution: The curve rises through \((-\tfrac12,0)\) and \((0, 5\ln3)\), hugging the asymptote \(x=-\tfrac34\) as \(y\to-\infty\).
markScheme: B1 — correct shape in the first three quadrants, tending to a vertical asymptote
Dep B1 — curve passing through \(-0.5\) on the x-axis and no other x-axis point
Dep B1 — curve passing through \(5\ln 3\) oe on the y-axis and no other y-axis point
B1 — asymptote \(x=-\tfrac34\) oe stated or shown (independent mark)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: It is given that \(f(x) = \ln(2x+5)\) for \(x > a\), where \(a\) is a constant. Write down the least possible value of \(a\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Using your value of \(a\), write down the range of f.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: It is also given that \(g(x) = x^2+1\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). Using your value of \(a\), solve the equation \(fg(x) = 4\), giving your answers in exact form.

questions.statement:
It is given that \(\;f(x) = \ln(2x+5)\) for \(x > a\), where \(a\) is a constant.

(a) Write down the least possible value of \(a\). [1]

(b) Using your value of \(a\), write down the range of f. [1]

It is also given that \(g(x) = x^2+1\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

(c) Using your value of \(a\), solve the equation \(fg(x) = 4\). Give your answers in exact form. [3]
tips: (a) \(\ln\) needs a positive input: \(2x+5>0 \Rightarrow x>-\tfrac52\), so the least \(a\) is \(-\tfrac52\).
(b) Over its full domain a ln function takes ALL real values: range \(f\in\mathbb{R}\).
(c) Build the composite: \(fg(x) = \ln(2(x^2+1)+5) = \ln(2x^2+7)\). Undo ln with e: \(2x^2+7 = e^4\).
(c) "Exact form" → \(x = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{e^4-7}{2}}\) — keep the ±, both work since \(g\) is even.
